en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Mount Guifeng during the Tang Dynasty.
The principles and analogies of the ten preceding points are clearly evident;

yet, when one carefully compares and examines the three teachings of Chan and the three teachings of the doctrinal schools, their relative shallowness and depth are as certain as a scale or a bushel measure. First, the Chan gate is described, and subsequently, by means of...
Regarding the scriptural evidence:
as for the three schools of Chan,
the first is the school of quelling delusions and cultivating the mind.
Second is the school of the ultimate extinction beyond reliance;
third is the school that directly reveals the nature of the mind.
Regarding these three types of teachings:
1. The teaching that, with intentional meaning, explains characteristics based on the nature;
2. The teaching that, with intentional meaning, refutes characteristics to reveal the nature;
3. The teaching that reveals the true mind as being identical to the nature.
These three teachings are to be verified one by one in relation to the preceding three schools respectively, as listed above.
Thereafter, they are all synthesized into a single flavor.
For now, I shall first describe the Chan school.
First, regarding the school that cultivates the mind by quelling delusions:

it teaches that although sentient beings inherently possess Buddha-nature, they fail to see it because it is obscured by beginningless ignorance; consequently, they transmigrate through birth and death.
Because all Buddhas have already severed delusive thoughts, they perceive their nature with perfect clarity;
having transcended birth and death, their supernormal powers are sovereign and free.
One should know that the functions of ordinary beings and sages differ.
External objects and the internal mind each have their own limits;
therefore, one must rely on the verbal instructions of a teacher to turn away from objects and contemplate the mind, thereby extinguishing deluded thoughts.
When these thoughts are exhausted, one awakens to the state of omniscience.
It is like a mirror obscured by dust;
one must diligently wipe it clean.
When the dust is exhausted and its clarity manifests, there is nothing it does not illuminate.
Furthermore, one must clearly understand the skillful means for entering the meditative state.
Remaining far removed from clamor and dwelling in a secluded, quiet place,
one should regulate the body and the breath, sitting cross-legged in silent repose.
With the tongue pressed against the upper palate and the mind focused on a single object,
the lineages of Nan-sheng, Bei-xiu, Bao-tang, Xuan-shi,
and others were all of this sort.
The approaches and skillful means employed by Niutou, Tiantai, Hui稠 (Hui-chou), Guṇabhadra, and others were largely the same; however,
their views and understandings differed.
Second, the school of "Exhaustive Extinction with No Basis" asserts that all phenomena,
whether mundane or supramundane,
are like dreams and illusions, being entirely non-existent.
Originally empty and quiescent, it has not become non-existent only now;
even this wisdom that realizes such non-existence is ungraspable.
In the equal Dharma-realm, there is no Buddha.
There are no sentient beings;
the dharma-realm is likewise a mere designation.
Since the mind does not exist, [so too do these].
Who says that in the dharma-realm there is neither cultivation nor non-cultivation, neither Buddha nor non-Buddha?
Even if there were a single dharma superior to nirvana,
I would say it is likewise like a dream or an illusion.
There is no dharma that can be grasped and no Buddha that can be made.
Whatever is created is entirely delusion and falsehood.
To realize this is to understand that, from the very beginning, there is nothing to be done.
When the mind has no place of reliance, one is finally free from inversion;
this is what is first called liberation.
From Shitou and Niutou down to Jingshan, [the lineage continues].
All [the Buddhas] demonstrate this principle,
thereby causing the mind and its activities to correspond with it,
and not allowing the emotions to become stagnant in any single dharma.
When practice has been sustained for a long time and merit reaches its culmination, habitual tendencies naturally vanish.
Thus, one becomes entirely unimpeded toward enemies and kin, suffering and pleasure;
from this, there arises—
A certain class of Daoist practitioners, Confucian scholars, and idle monks who engage in superficial inquiry into the principles of Chan all speak these words;
they consider them to be the ultimate attainment, yet they do not know this school.
Not only do we take these words as the Dharma;
the schools of Heze, Jiangxi, Tiantai, and others also expound this principle,
yet it is not what they primarily uphold.
Third, as for the school that directly reveals the nature of the mind:
it teaches that all phenomena, whether existent or empty, are solely the true nature;
this true nature is signless and unconditioned.
Its essence is not any thing whatsoever—
meaning it is neither ordinary nor holy, neither cause nor fruit, neither good nor evil,
and so forth. Nevertheless, through the functioning of that very essence, it is able to produce all manner of things.
This refers to the ability to manifest as ordinary beings or as noble ones, and to manifest forms, marks, and so forth.
Within this, the nature of the mind is pointed out;
furthermore, there are two categories.
One version states:
That which is currently capable of speech, movement, desire, anger, compassion, patience, performing good or evil deeds, and experiencing suffering or pleasure—
this is your Buddha-nature.
This very [mind] is fundamentally the Buddha;
apart from this, there is no other Buddha.
To realize this is to understand that it is the true, heavenly, and spontaneous nature.
Therefore, one should not give rise to the thought of cultivating the Way;
the Way is itself the mind.
One cannot take the mind to cultivate the mind.
Evil is also the mind;
one cannot use the mind to sever the mind.
Without severing or cultivating, there is spontaneous mastery.
This alone is called liberation.
Its nature is like space, neither increasing nor decreasing;
what need is there for supplementation?
Simply cease all activity at all times and in all places;
nourish the sacred embryo of the spirit so that it may grow and manifest its spontaneous, divine wondrousness.
This is precisely what constitutes true awakening, true cultivation, and true realization.
Second, it is said that all phenomena are like dreams;
this is the common teaching of all the sages.
Therefore, deluded thoughts are fundamentally quiescent and sensory objects are fundamentally empty.
Within this empty and quiescent mind, spiritual awareness is not obscured.
It is precisely this empty and quiescent awareness that [is the true nature].
This is your true nature.
Whether deluded or awakened, the mind fundamentally knows itself;
it does not arise dependent on conditions nor is it triggered by objects.
The single word "knowing" is the gateway to all wonders.
Because of beginningless delusion regarding it,
one falsely clings to the body and mind as a self, giving rise to thoughts of greed, anger, and the like.
If one encounters a virtuous friend who provides instruction,
one suddenly awakens to the knowledge of emptiness and quiescence;
this knowledge is itself without thought and without form.
Who is it that perceives the mark of self and the mark of person?
When one awakens to the emptiness of all marks, the mind is naturally free from thought;
if a thought arises, one immediately awakens to it.
To awaken to this is the wondrous gate of non-practice; it lies solely herein.
Therefore, although one fully cultivates the myriad practices, one takes non-thought as the primary principle.
If one merely attains the knowledge and vision of non-thought,
then love and hatred will naturally become tranquil and thin,
while compassion and wisdom will naturally increase and become clear.
Karmic offenses will naturally be severed,
and meritorious practice will naturally increase.
Having realized that all marks are non-marks, one attains liberation.
This is the natural cultivation of non-cultivation.
When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are immediately severed.
Once arising and ceasing have been extinguished—
When quiescent illumination manifests before one, its application is inexhaustible;
this is what is called "Buddha.
Thus, both of these schools converge upon phenomena to return to their fundamental nature.
Therefore, they belong to the same school.
Nevertheless, within these three aforementioned schools,
there are further those who follow the teachings and those who are arrogant toward the teachings.
It follows after characteristics while subverting those very characteristics;
it serves as a gateway for repelling external challenges and provides skillful means for engaging with external multitudes.
The ritual procedures for instructing disciples vary in many ways;
all of them are gateways to the practice of the two benefits, each according to what is most convenient.
Nor is there anything lost;
it is simply that the principles one adheres to cannot logically be dualistic.
Therefore, it is necessary to harmonize them based on the Buddha’s own teaching.
Next, the classification of the Buddha’s teachings into three types is as follows:

First, the teaching that explains characteristics based on the underlying intention of the nature; herein, the Buddha perceives the three realms and the six destinies as all being the manifestations of true nature.
However, sentient beings delude their own nature and give rise [to afflictions];
they have no separate self-substance.
Therefore, it is said that they "rely upon nature."
However, those with dull faculties find it difficult to achieve sudden awakening.
Therefore, one preaches the Dharma according to the objective appearances perceived by each individual to gradually lead them across.
Hence, it is called "preaching the signs" (*lakṣaṇadeśanā*).
Because it has not yet been fully revealed, it is called "profound intention" (*samdhāya-bhāṣita*). Within this teaching, there are three categories.
The first is the teaching on the causes and effects of humans and devas, which explains the retribution of good and evil karma so that one may know that cause and effect do not fail.
Fearing the sufferings of the three miserable realms and seeking the happiness of the human and celestial realms,
one cultivates all virtuous practices such as generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration,
thereby attaining rebirth in the human realm, the celestial realms, and even the form and formless realms.
This is called the teaching for humans and devas.
Second is the teaching on severing delusions and extinguishing suffering and pleasure,
which explains that the three realms are unstable and entirely as painful as a burning house.
It causes the cessation of the accumulation of karma and afflictions;
because the cultivation of the path and the realization of cessation accord with individual capacities,
the number of dharmas taught varies accordingly.
By this, one distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox;
by this, one discerns between the ordinary and the sage;
by this, one differentiates between what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed.
To clarify cause and effect,
it is taught that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings are entirely devoid of a self or a master;
they are all merely the physical form of matter.
The thinking mind,
due to the power of causes and conditions from time immemorial,
arises and perishes moment by moment in an endless succession.
Like a stream of water trickling away,
like the flickering of a lamp’s flame,
the body and mind are a provisional union that appears to be one and appears to be permanent.
Ordinary fools, failing to realize this, grasp at it as a self.

Because they cherish this self, they give rise to the three poisons: greed for fame, profit, and honor; hatred toward objects that oppose the self and fear of being harmed by them; and delusion, which consists of misapprehension, irrational calculations, and the like.
The three poisons strike the mental consciousness, inciting the body and speech to create all manner of karma.

Because karma is difficult to escape—just as a shadow follows a form and an echo responds to a sound—one undergoes bodies of pleasure and pain within the five destinies; this is what is produced by individual karma. The various superior and inferior locations within the triple world where one dwells are what is produced by collective karma. Regarding the body thus received, one again clings to it as a self.
Returning again, they give rise to greed and other afflictions, creating karma and undergoing retribution;
their bodies then experience birth, old age, sickness, and death,
dying only to be born once more.
The realms thus undergo formation, abiding, destruction,
and emptiness; from emptiness they form again,
such that birth after birth and kalpa after kalpa, the cycle of saṃsāra continues without end.
Without beginning and without end, it is like a waterwheel;

this is entirely due to not realizing that this body is fundamentally not the self. All of the above concerns the causes and effects of the world within the teachings of the former human and celestial realms.
Previously, it merely caused one to feel weary of the lower realms and to rejoice in the higher;
it did not yet state that all three realms are to be viewed with weariness,
nor did it yet refute the self.
I shall now explain this in full:
it refers to the two truths of suffering and its origin.
Below, the text refutes the grasping at a self to lead one to cultivate the two truths of cessation and the path.
It clarifies the causes and effects of transcending the world;
therefore, it is called the teaching of the Four Noble Truths.
That which is not the self is this body, whose fundamental cause is the characteristic of the union of form and mind.

Now, through investigation and analysis, we find that form consists of four categories: earth, water, fire, and wind. Mind consists of four categories: feeling, which experiences pleasant and unpleasant things;

perception, which grasps images; formations, which perform all volitional constructions; and consciousness, which individually cognizes each object. These four, together with form, are collectively termed the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). If all of these were the self, [it would follow that the self is manifold].
Thus, there would be eight "selves.
Furthermore, within form there are three hundred and sixty segments of bone;

each segment is distinct, and the skin, hair, flesh, sinews, liver, heart, lungs, and kidneys are each different from one another. Skin is not hair, and so forth; all these mental factors (caitasika) are likewise each distinct.
Seeing is not hearing;
joy is not anger.
Since there are already these many things, [how can they be one?]
One does not know for certain which of these should be taken as the self.
If all of them were the self,
then within a single body consisting of hundreds or thousands of parts, there would be the confusion of many masters.
Apart from this, there is no other distinct phenomenon.
When one turns this over and examines it for a "self," it cannot be found at all.
One then realizes that this body, mind, and so forth are all merely a collection of various conditions appearing as a composite; they are fundamentally not a single entity.
These semblances of self and person are fundamentally not self or person;
for whom, then, is there greed and anger?
For whom, then, is there killing and stealing?

Whoever cultivates the precepts and generosity, whoever is born among humans or devas, and who knows suffering and its origin, will ultimately not allow the mind to stagnate within the outflows of the three realms. By severing the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*), they cultivate only the wisdom of the contemplation of non-self—the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)—to sever greed and the like, thereby bringing all karmic activities to rest.
He realized the True Suchness of Self-Emptiness, attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, and eventually, having extinguished all afflictions and burdens, attained the fruit of Arhatship.

Through the Truth of Cessation, he dissolved his physical body and extinguished his cognitive faculties, forever departing from all suffering. This is recorded in the six hundred and eighteen volumes of the Āgamas and other scriptures.

The six hundred and ninety-eight fascicles of treatises, such as the *Vibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, all exclusively expound upon these Small Vehicle teachings and the causes and effects of the preceding stages of humans and devas;

though the volumes are numerous, their principles do not transcend this. Third, the teaching that uses consciousness to refute objects explains the characteristics of the objects previously described.
Whether arising or ceasing,
it is not only devoid of self,
but also lacks such phenomena as those mentioned above.
However, these are merely delusive transformations arising from emotional consciousness;
therefore, it is said that "consciousness is used to penetrate objects. When the aforementioned dharmas of arising and ceasing are discussed, they do not pertain to True Suchness (tathatā).
Rather, each sentient being has, since beginningless time, naturally possessed eight kinds of consciousness as their fundamental nature.
Among these, the eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is their fundamental basis;
it suddenly transforms the seeds of the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world.
The seven consciousnesses arise in turn;
each is able to manifest its own respective objects of perception,
from the eye perceiving forms up to the seventh perceiving the eighth as its object.
The eight conditions—the sense organs (*indriya*), seeds (*bīja*), and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*)—are entirely devoid of real dharmas external to these eight consciousnesses.
Question: How do they undergo transformation?
Answer: Through the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and dharmas.
When the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as a semblance of self and phenomena.
Because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are shrouded by ignorance,
they take these appearances as objects and grasp them as a real self and real phenomena.

Just as when one is afflicted by illness, the mind becomes heavy and one perceives various colors, people, and objects in dreams; what is seen therein can be understood as being due to the power of the dream-illness,
whereby the mind manifests appearances resembling various external objects.
During a dream, one grasps at external objects as being truly existent;
only upon waking does one realize they were merely transformations produced by the dream.
So it is with this body of mine and external objects.
It is likewise so.
It is merely what is transformed by consciousness;
due to delusion, one clings to the existence of a self and various objects.
Having realized that fundamentally there is no self or phenomena, but only mind and consciousness,

one then relies on this wisdom of the two emptinesses to cultivate the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as well as the practices of the six perfections and the four means of attraction.
Gradually subduing and severing the two obstacles— the afflictive and the cognitive—
one realizes the true suchness (tathatā) manifested by the two kinds of emptiness,
and the ten stages (bhūmis) reach completion.
The transformation of the eight consciousnesses results in the four wisdoms of bodhi.
When the obstructions to true suchness are exhausted,
one achieves the Dharma-nature body of Great Nirvana.
The principles expounded in dozens of sūtras, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*,
and in hundreds of fascicles of treatises, such as the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
It does not go beyond this.
These three preceding categories together constitute the first type of teaching: the teaching that explains characteristics based on the nature through intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
However, only the third is the teaching that uses consciousness to refute [the reality of] objects.
This accords with and complements the Chan school’s principle of quelling delusions and cultivating the mind.
Because one knows that external objects are entirely empty, one does not cultivate the phenomenal characteristics of external objects;
rather, one solely quiets delusions and cultivates the mind.
"Cessation of delusion" means the cessation of the delusions regarding self and dharmas.
"Cultivation of the mind" means...
Because they cultivate the mind of *vijñapti-mātra*,
they accord with the teaching of *vijñapti-mātra*.
Since they are thus identical to the Buddha, [they are one with him].

How could one disparage the gradual gate of destroying delusions, which involves observing purity and constantly wiping away [impurities], concentrating the mind and dwelling the mind, focusing single-mindedly on a single object, as well as cross-legged sitting, regulating the body, and regulating the breath?
All these various skillful means are entirely those which the Buddha has exhorted and praised.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
It is not necessary to sit, nor is it necessary not to sit.
Whether sitting or not sitting, act in accordance with the appropriate occasion;
concentrate or direct the mind as each person’s own capacity and disposition allow.
During the reigns of Emperor Gaozong and up until the era of Emperor Xuanzong,
the Perfect and Sudden school of our own tradition had not yet spread to the northern lands;
only Master Shenxiu extensively propagated the teachings of gradualism.
He served as the Dharma Lord of the two capitals and the Gate Teacher of three emperors;
he fully upheld the school of Daruma,
yet did not manifest the principle that one is inherently Buddha.
Caoshui and Heze,
fearing that the Perfect Teaching (yuanzong) would perish,
consequently reviled and rejected practices such as "abiding in the mind" and "subduing the mind."
However, this is for the purpose of curing illness;
it is not for the purpose of removing the Dharma.
Moreover, this expedient means was originally taught by the Great Master, the Fifth Patriarch.
Each was certified as a master of a particular quarter.
Bodhidharma taught people to settle the mind through "wall-contemplation":
externally ceasing all conditions and internally ensuring the mind is free from agitation.
If the mind is like a wall or a screen, one can enter the Way;
is this not precisely the method for seated meditation?
Furthermore, there are two fascicles of the *Dharmatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra* translated by the Master of Mount Lu, Huiyuan, together with the two Indian monks Buddhayaśas and Buddhabhadra.
The gradual expedients for the gateway of seated meditation (dhyāna) possessed by Juming were in no way different from the intent of the Tiantai school and the disciples of Yi and Xiù; thus,
for several decades, the Fourth Patriarch did not let his side touch the mat.
One thus understands that the tenets of "realization" and "non-realization" each depend on the depth or shallowness of one's insight;
they are not determined by whether one's conduct is disciplined or undisciplined.
The partial and the perfect merely serve as remedies according to the specific ailment;
there is no need to praise this or disparage that. This concludes the preceding introduction.
Someone raised an objection to me, saying:
Why do I encourage those who practice seated meditation?
I now answer this with two points of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): the teaching that shatters appearances to reveal the nature is based on the ultimate, definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus, since deluded attachments are fundamentally empty from the outset, there is nothing further to be shattered.
The untainted dharmas are fundamentally the true nature;
their wondrous functioning in accordance with conditions is forever uninterrupted and should not be destroyed.

However, because a certain class of sentient beings clings to false appearances and obstructs the true nature, making it difficult for them to attain profound awakening, the Buddha has, for the time being,
not distinguished between good and evil or defilement and purity, but has instead refuted all such natures and characteristics.
Because true nature and its wondrous function are not non-existent,
yet one says they are "non-existent," it is therefore called "intentional meaning" (*saṃdhāya*).
Furthermore, the intention lies in revealing the nature (dharmatā),
while the words serve to dismantle appearances (lakṣaṇa). Thus,
the intention is not fully manifested within the words.

Therefore, it is called "esoteric. Since the objects manifested within the previously explained teachings are all illusory and false, how could the consciousness that manifests them be anything other than unreal?
This is because mind and object depend upon one another, being empty yet appearing as if they exist.
Furthermore, the mind does not arise in isolation;
it arises only by depending upon objects.
Objects do not arise of themselves.
They manifest due to the mind;
when the mind is empty, the objects vanish.
When the objects cease, the mind becomes empty.
There has never been a mind without an object,
nor has there ever been an object without a mind;
it is like seeing things in a dream, where there appears to be a distinction between the seer and the seen.
In reality, this same delusion is entirely non-existent.
All consciousnesses and all objects are likewise so,
because they are all provisionally dependent upon various conditions and lack intrinsic nature.
There has never been a single dharma that was not born from causes and conditions;
therefore, there is no dharma whatsoever that is not empty.
All marks that exist are entirely illusory.
Therefore, in emptiness there is no form;
there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind;
and there are no eighteen elements.
There is no twelvefold chain of dependent origination;
there are no four noble truths;
there is no wisdom.
Furthermore, there is no attainment,
no karma, and no retribution.
There is no cultivation and no realization;
birth-and-death and nirvana are equal, like an illusion.
One simply takes as the practice of the Way the non-abiding in all things, characterized by non-grasping and non-attachment.
This is the teaching found in the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras totaling over a thousand fascicles,
as well as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and other such works.
The *Three Treatises*, the *Extensive Hundred Treatise* (*Śata-śāstra*),
and others all explain this; the *Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom* (*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) in one hundred fascicles likewise explains this principle.

However, because the Master [Xuanzang] thoroughly realized and did not cling [to these distinctions], he encompassed both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna systems of *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) within his final school of True Nature (*tathatā*). Thus, this teaching is entirely identical to the Chan School’s school of "Exhaustion and Non-reliance."
Since this is what was taught by the World-Honored One himself and what Bodhisattvas propagate,
why is it that whenever the masters of gradualist meditation and their disciples hear this teaching, [they react as they do]?
They immediately slandered [him], saying,
"He denies cause and effect.
The Buddha himself said:
"There is no karma and no retribution—
how can this not be a false view?
If you say that the Buddha spoke these words with a profound underlying meaning,"
Could it be that this teaching of the Chan school lacks profound meaning?
If you say, "I have examined and scrutinized awakening and found no profound meaning," that is simply because you have encountered those who do not understand.
One may merely criticize the person;
how could one ever disparage the Dharma?
Although the preceding teaching, when considered according to the Buddha’s original intent, does not contradict this.
Subsequently, those who transmitted the teachings mostly clung to the literal text while losing sight of the essential meaning.
Some adhered to individual views and mutually refuted one another;
others believed in both indiscriminately, remaining muddled and ignorant.
Therefore, bodhisattvas such as Nāgārjuna and Āryadeva,
relying on the teachings that deconstruct appearances, extensively expounded the meaning of emptiness;
they shattered their attachment to existence so that [beings] might gain a clear and penetrating understanding of true emptiness.
Emptiness in the sense of "true emptiness" is the emptiness that does not contradict existence.
Bodhisattvas such as Asanga and Vasubandhu extensively explained names and characteristics based on the teaching of Consciousness-Only.
By analyzing that characteristics and appearances are distinct and that defilement and purity are each separate,
one shatters their attachment to emptiness and causes them to clearly understand wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*).
Wondrous existence is existence that does not contradict emptiness.
Although each [master] expounds a single meaning, they do so while fully embodying the entire system;
therefore, there is no contradiction.
Question: If this is so, why is it that later masters such as Bhāviveka and Dharmapāla refuted one another?
Answer: This is actually mutual establishment, not mutual refutation. Why is this so?
Because the faculties of those who have only recently begun their studies are gradually becoming dull and they mutually cling to emptiness and existence,
Bhāviveka and others refute the characteristics of fixed existence,
causing them to penetrate thoroughly to ultimate, absolute emptiness.
Only then is that "wondrous existence" (miaoyou) of dependent origination established.

Dharmapāla and others refute the nihilistic view of biased emptiness with the intent of preserving this wondrous existence; because this wondrous existence is preserved, [the teaching of dependent origination is maintained].
This is precisely that non-substantiality of true emptiness. On the surface, the texts appear to contradict one another, yet in meaning, they mutually complement each other.

Having described the preceding doubts regarding the rivalry between the Southern and Northern Chan schools, this section now provides a definitive resolution. This is because the "wondrous existence" and "true emptiness" possess two interrelated meanings.
First, the meaning of extreme contradiction,
which refers to mutual harm, total seizure,
and eternal exhaustion. Second, the meaning of extreme conformity.
This means that they are merged into a single characteristic, such that the entire substance is completely encompassed.
If they did not mutually subsume one another, there would be nothing at all;
because the entire substance is fully contained within each, that which is most contradictory is precisely what is most harmonious.
Nāgārjuna, Asaṅga, and others establish [their positions] from the perspective of ultimate conformity;
Bhāviveka, Dharmapāla, and others refute [them] based on the perspective of ultimate contradiction.
Thus, they are unimpeded in their ability to establish or refute according to the freedom of either contradiction or conformity.
Thus, there is nothing among all phenomena that is not in accord.
Alas! The later students of the sūtras and śāstras within these two schools here have come to treat one another with mutual disparagement and repudiation, no different from mortal enemies.
When shall we attain the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Now, those who practice the sudden and gradual methods of Chan are also like this;
exert yourselves to gain comprehensive insight and do not remain partial or narrow-minded.
Question: Since the sages of the Western Regions refuted one another yet ultimately achieved mutual completion, how can it be that those of this region,
while disagreeing with one another, have instead come to harbor mutual jealousy?
The answer is: It is like a person drinking water—the coldness or warmth is known by oneself.
Each must observe their own mind and each must examine their own thoughts.
Taking medicine to prevent illness does not constitute being a person in good health.
Establishing laws to prevent wickedness is not for the sake of the worthy and virtuous.

Third, it reveals the true mind as the very nature; this teaching of the direct pointing to one's own mind indicates that the self-mind is itself the true nature, rather than indicating it by means of phenomenal appearances.
Nor is it shown by way of restricting it to the characteristics of the mind;
therefore, it is said to be "identical with nature" (*jìngxìng*).
This is not a matter of expedient means or hidden secrecy.
Therefore, it is said that this teaching reveals that all sentient beings possess a true mind of emptiness and quiescence;
from the beginningless past, its nature has been inherently pure, and it does not become pure through the severing of delusions.
Therefore, it is said that its nature is pure.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"Purity is twofold."
First, purity of intrinsic nature;
second, purity through the removal of defilements.
As the Śrīmālādevī-sūtra says:
The intrinsically pure mind is difficult to comprehend;
that this very mind is defiled by afflictions is likewise difficult to comprehend.
The commentary states:
This mind transcends the principles of the two preceding schools—the Śūnyavāda and the Satyadvaya (existence)—and is therefore difficult to comprehend.

It is luminously clear and never obscured; it is ever-present awareness. The passage below cites the Buddha’s teaching that it remains eternally present and indestructible throughout the limits of the future.
It is called Buddha-nature;
it is also called the Tathāgatagarbha;
it is also called the Mind-ground. This is the very mind transmitted by the Dharma, which has been obscured by delusive conceptualization since beginningless time.
Failing to realize this for themselves, they become attached to birth and death.
Out of great compassion, the Great Awakened One appeared in the world and taught that all phenomena, including birth and death, are entirely empty.
It is revealed that this mind is entirely identical to that of all Buddhas.
As the "Chapter on the Manifestation" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"O Son of the Buddha..."
There is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
yet, because they are all equally attached through deluded conceptualization, they do not realize it.
If one were free from deluded conceptualization...
The knowledge of all things,
spontaneous knowledge,
and unimpeded knowledge.

This is immediately manifested before one, as illustrated by the analogy of a great scripture: the measure of the Buddha’s wisdom is equal to the three-thousandfold world system; the essence of that wisdom is boundless and its circumference encompasses the entire Dharma-realm. Just as it records all events within the three-thousandfold world system exhaustively, this illustrates that upon the essence there are inherently present merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This great sutra scroll,
although its magnitude equals that of the trichiliocosm,
dwells entirely within a single minute atom; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom.
It is fully and perfectly complete within the bodies of all sentient beings; just as one sentient being serves as an example for a single atom, so it is with every atom.
At that time, there was a person whose wisdom was clear and penetrating like that of the World-Honored One, who had fully attained the pure divine eye.
With the power of his divine eye, he saw this sutra scroll within a mote of dust, perceiving forms through obstructions.

This is like the power of the Buddha-eye seeing the Buddha-wisdom through the veil of afflictions; it is like being of no benefit whatsoever to sentient beings when one is deluded and thus fails to utilize it.

It is not different from non-existence, yet one immediately employs skillful means to shatter those subtle particles—this is like preaching the Dharma to eliminate obstacles and bring forth this great sutra-scroll.
It causes all sentient beings to universally obtain benefit, and so forth, even unto the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is likewise thus.

It is immeasurable and unimpeded, universally able to benefit all sentient beings; it encompasses the events of the three thousandfold world-system in their entirety within the bodies of sentient beings, and even within a single minute particle. Yet, all ordinary, ignorant people harbor deluded thoughts and cling to them.
Unaware and unconscious, they fail to obtain benefit.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure eye of wisdom,
universally observes all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.
And he spoke these words:
"How marvelous, how marvelous!
These sentient beings."
"How is it that they possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata,
yet through folly and delusion they neither know nor see?
I shall instruct them in the Noble Path."
He causes them to be forever free from delusive thoughts and attachments,
so that within their own bodies they may perceive the vast wisdom of the Tathāgata as no different from that of a Buddha.
He then instructs those sentient beings to practice the noble path— the six *pāramitās*, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and so forth— thereby causing them to abandon delusive thoughts.
Having abandoned false conceptualization, one realizes the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata, which brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
Question: Since it was stated above that the nature is inherently lucid and constantly cognizant, [how can there be delusion?]
What need is there for the Buddhas to provide instruction?
The answer to this is that "knowing" does not refer to realized knowledge (*pratyātmajñāna*).
The intended meaning is that true nature is not the same as empty space or wood and stone;
therefore, it is said to "know.
It is not like the consciousness that discriminates when encountering objects.
It is not like the wisdom that realizes through the act of illumination;
it is simply the nature of true suchness itself,
which is spontaneously and eternally aware.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa said:
"Tathatā is the true, intrinsic awareness of reality.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the Chapter on Dedication (*Parivarta*), also says:
Its nature is the illumination of *tathatā*.
Furthermore, according to the "Chapter on Clarifying Questions" (*Pṛcchāmukhaparivarta*),
it is stated that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) are distinct.
Wisdom is restricted to the sagely and does not extend to the ordinary;
knowledge exists in both the ordinary and the sagely and extends to both principle and phenomena.
Therefore, the nine bodhisattvas, beginning with Bodhirāja, asked Mañjuśrī:
"What is the wisdom that realizes the Buddha-realm? What is the wisdom that knows the primordially existing true mind within the Buddha-realm? Mañjuśrī answered regarding this wisdom:
The wisdom of all Buddhas is sovereign and unimpeded throughout the three periods of time; there is no matter of the past, future, or present that they do not fully comprehend.
Therefore, their responses are sovereign and unobstructed, as it is said: "They know."
That which cannot be known by consciousness and is not an object of consciousness is so because consciousness belongs to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*),
and conceptual discrimination is not true knowledge.
True knowledge is solely non-thought;
only then is it seen. It is not the realm of the mind and cannot be known by wisdom.
This means that if one were to attempt to realize it through wisdom, [it would remain ungraspable].
This would then belong to the realm of that which is realized.
Since true knowledge is not an object,
it cannot be realized by means of cognition.
A mind that arises in a flash and reflects is not true knowledge.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The self-mind grasps the self-mind;
that which is not illusion becomes illusory phenomena.
As the Treatise says:
The mind does not perceive the mind.
Master Heze said:
"To direct the mind toward it is already a deviation."
Therefore, the Northern School’s practice of "observing the mind" deviates from the true intent.
If the mind can be observed,
it becomes an object of perception.

Therefore, it is said that this is not the domain of the mind; its nature is fundamentally pure (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), not requiring the removal of defilements and delusions to become pure, nor requiring the severance of the turbidity of doubt to become clear.
Hence, it is called "fundamentally pure."
In the *Ratnagotravibhāga*,
it is distinguished that this is not the purity of being free from defilement,
but rather the intrinsic purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*) of that very nature.
Therefore it is said:
"Its nature is fundamentally pure, revealing this to all sentient beings.
Since it is said to be fundamentally pure, it does not depend upon the severing of hindrances.
One immediately knows that all sentient beings possess [this nature] from the very beginning;
it is only because they are obscured by delusion that they do not realize it themselves.
Therefore, the Buddha reveals and teaches it so that all may awaken and enter into it.
This refers to the opening, revealing, awakening to, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as cited above.
The Buddha appeared in the world solely for this purpose.
He says:
"That which is made pure" refers to the stainless purity within the *ratnagotra* (the Jewel Nature).
Although this mind is pure by its very nature,
one must ultimately realize and cultivate it before its essential nature and phenomenal characteristics can attain perfect purity; thus,
there are dozens of sutras and treatises [on this subject].
All [scriptures] speak of two kinds of purity and two kinds of liberation.
Yet, those of shallow learning nowadays may know only the purity of being free from defilement.
Because they have attained the liberation of stainless purity,
they disparage the gates of dhyāna as being "mind itself is Buddha," or they know only the intrinsic purity of self-nature.
Because they regard the liberation of intrinsic purity as supreme,
they treat the formal aspects of the teachings with contempt and disparage the upholding of the Vinaya.
Those who practice such disciplines as sitting meditation and self-restraint do not realize that one must suddenly awaken to the self-nature of purity, which is inherently liberated;
rather, they gradually cultivate it to attain the purity of being free from defilement.
Being liberated from hindrances,
one achieves perfect, pure, and ultimate liberation;
whether in body or mind, there is no obstruction or stagnation.
This is the same as for Śākyamuni Buddha.
The *Pao-tsang lun* (Treasure Store Treatise) also says:
"To know that existence has destruction."
To know non-existence as non-existent and not to fail in this—these are all the wisdom that knows existence and non-existence, the knowledge of true knowing.

When existence and non-existence are not reckoned, and one neither reckons existence nor non-existence, there is the knowledge of self-nature free from conceptual differentiation. Thus is the mind of numinous awareness revealed.
This is precisely because true nature is no different from the Buddha;
therefore, it reveals that the True Mind is itself the Nature-Teaching (*dharmatā-deśanā*).
This includes more than forty sūtras, such as the *Avataṃsaka*, *Ghanavyūha*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, *Tathāgatagarbha*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Although the fifteen treatises— including the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, the *Tathāgatagarbha*, the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Daśabhūmika*, and the *Dharmadhātu-nirvāṇa*—
differ in being either sudden or gradual,
they all belong to this teaching (the Dharma-Ending Age) insofar as they reveal the essential nature of phenomena.
The third school of the Chan gate is the doctrine that directly reveals the nature of mind.
Since Aśvaghoṣa designated the mind as the fundamental source,
and Mañjuśrī identified knowing as the true essence.
How can those who deconstruct appearances merely speak of quiescent extinction while disallowing true knowledge?
As for those who propound appearances—
Those who hold that ordinary people differ from sages do not allow that one is immediately a Buddha.
Now, based on the Buddhist teachings, we determine that the primary purpose [of this transmission] is for such persons.
Therefore, the previous account of the transmission of the mind in the Western Regions shows that it was largely combined with the sutras and śāstras, without being divided into two separate paths.
However, because those deluded minds of this land cling to the literal text and take the name as the essence, Dharmatrāta skillfully selected the words to transmit the mind.

He set forth its name—stating that "mind" is the name—and silently indicated its essence—making it known that "this" is the mind. He used the metaphor of "wall-contemplation," as described above, to cause all conditions to cease.
Question: When all conditions are severed, is there cessation?
Answer: Although all thoughts are severed, there is no cessation.
Question: By what means of verification is it known that there is no cessation?
When he answered that he knew it clearly himself and that words could not reach it,
the Master immediately certified him, saying:
"This very state is the intrinsically pure mind."
Do not harbor further doubts.
If what has been answered does not accord with your understanding,
simply set aside all that is incorrect and continue to investigate further.
Ultimately, one does not first communicate the knowledge of this word to others;
rather, it is only upon attaining self-awakening that its reality is verified—
this constitutes the direct realization of its essence.
Thereafter, he sealed [the transmission] to sever all remaining doubts;
hence it is said:
"The mind-seal is transmitted in silence."
As for what is called "silence," it refers only to knowing the word "silent";
it does not mean total silence.
This has been the case throughout the transmission from generation to generation down to the time of Heze,
when the other schools vied with one another to propagate their teachings;
those seeking a silent resonance found no corresponding karmic conditions.
Furthermore, he reflected upon the "suspended-thread" prophecy concerning the Dharma, in which Bodhidharma said:
"After the sixth generation of my Dharma,
my life will be like a suspended thread, and I fear that the fundamental tenets of our school will perish."
He thus explicitly stated that the single word "knowledge" (zhi) is the gateway to all wonders,
leaving it to practitioners to realize its depth according to their own capacity,
while he devoted himself to ensuring that the transmission of the religious teachings would not be interrupted.
This is also due to the arrival of the destiny of this country’s great Dharma-cycle.
Because a class of both monastics and laypeople were able to hear it universally, the response was such as this.
As for those who transmitted it silently, others did not know of it.
Therefore, the *kāṣāya* is taken as the token of faith;
those who transmit it openly are easily distinguished by their disciples.
One merely uses words and explanations to dispel doubts.
Moreover, since these words have already been expressed, they are sufficient to cite as scriptural and doctrinal proof for the external objection previously stated:
"Do those who transmit the Dharma nowadays speak in esoteric language?
This is the answer provided here.
The Dharma is the dharma of the *dharma*-nature;
therefore, those who hear it all benefit, whether their capacity be shallow or deep.
It is simply that what was formerly secret is now revealed.
Therefore, it is not called "esoteric language.
Could it be that the distinct phenomena are also distinct? Having awakened to this mind, how should one practice it?
Should one still rely on the instructions regarding signs (*nimitta*) as first explained and engage in seated meditation (*dhyāna*)?
The answer to this has two points:
namely, that lethargy is so dense and heavy that it is difficult to rouse,
and that agitation is so violent and sharp that it cannot be suppressed.
For those whose greed and anger are blazing and difficult to restrain when encountering sensory objects,
one should employ the various skillful means from the aforementioned teachings to subdue them according to their specific ailments. If,
however, their afflictions are slight and their wisdom and understanding are clear and sharp, [one should proceed accordingly].
This is based on the One-Practice Samādhi of our own school’s fundamental teachings.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"If one cultivates cessation (*śamatha*):"
Dwelling in a quiet place, with body upright and mind rectified, one does not rely on inhalation and exhalation or on forms and colors;
eventually, there is only mind, free from external objects.
The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states:
Dhyāna is movement and non-movement; non-dhyāna is the dhyāna of non-arising.
The *Dharmapada* says:
"If one studies various samādhis..."
This movement is not sitting meditation;
when the mind flows following after objects,
how can it be called concentration?
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"To manifest all dignified postures— walking, standing, sitting, and reclining— without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and to manifest neither body nor mind within the triple world (the three realms)—
this is true seated meditation."
This is the body sealed by the Buddha;
based on this, he answered:
"The three realms are like flowers in the sky; the four modes of birth are but dreams and slumber."
Relying on the essence, one gives rise to practice that is non-practice;
yet, one dwells neither in Buddhahood nor in the mind.
Who would then discuss the higher or lower realms? As previously stated in the objection:

As for those who, relying on the teachings, insist that one must lead others to the meditative states of the higher realms, they are like one peering at the sky through a tube; they merely cling to the provisional doctrines of their own school.
Upon seeing this definitive teaching, they ought to feel shame and withdraw. For within this teaching, the single true mind-nature is set in contrast to all phenomena of both defilement and purity.
It is both a total exclusion and a total inclusion.
As for the total exclusion,
it is as explained above.
Directly pointing to the essence of the enlightened mind, it is precisely this spiritual awareness that is the nature of the mind;
all else is merely false and delusive.
Therefore it is said:
"It is not that which is cognized by consciousness;
it is not the mind, its objects, and so forth."
It extends even to being neither nature nor characteristic;
it is neither Buddha nor sentient being, transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations.
As for "completely encompassing":
All phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are none other than the mind.
Because the mind is deluded, it falsely gives rise to afflictions and karma,
extending even to the four modes of birth, the six realms of existence, and the impure world-realms.
Because the mind has attained awakening, it gives rise to function from its essence;
thus, the four immeasurables, the six perfections, up to the four analytical knowledges, the ten powers, the wondrous body, and the pure lands—
there is nothing that does not manifest.
Since all phenomena arise as manifestations of this mind,
all phenomena are entirely identical to the true mind,
just like the things manifested in a person's dream.
Every phenomenon is the person,
just as when gold is fashioned into vessels,
every vessel is gold.
Like reflections appearing in a mirror,
each reflection is a dream-like encounter with deluded thoughts and karmic retribution;
the vessel is a metaphor for spiritual practice.
Because the shadow is a metaphor for the manifested transformation, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"To know that all phenomena are the very nature of one's own mind is to achieve the body of wisdom,
which does not arise through awakening by means of another."
The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:
"The three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind;
apart from the mind, the objects of the six sense-fields do not exist."
Even all conceptual discriminations are simply the discrimination of one's own mind;
the mind does not perceive the mind.
No characteristic can be apprehended;
therefore, all phenomena are like reflections in a mirror.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says:
Quiescence is called the single mind;
the single mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
It is capable of universally producing and creating all realms of rebirth.
Because one experiences suffering and pleasure through the commission of good and evil deeds,
and because these are co-existent with their causes, it is known that nothing whatsoever is not mind.
This constitutes the "Exclusionary Gate" (*quan jian men*), which subsumes the second preceding teaching on the refutation of characteristics (*po xiang jiao*).
The "Gate of Complete Inclusion" subsumes the first teaching mentioned above, that of the Teaching of Characteristics;
when compared with this [present teaching],
it is utterly different from the former.
This [latter] subsumes the former;
the former is entirely identical to this.
The profound necessarily encompasses the shallow.
The shallow does not reach the deep.
Only when one directly reveals the essence of the true mind can one,
within that state, discern all things and encompass all things.
In this way, when one has attained mastery over the non-obstruction between essence and characteristics through such discernment,
one is then able to abide nowhere at all regarding all phenomena;
only this is called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
